_comment: Executable filename -> the component that ships it.
Read by identify-elf-presence.py alongside elf-soname-map.json. Where that map
reads a library's SONAME, this one reads the name a program is installed under.
A firmware that carries `/bin/dhcpcd` carries dhcpcd, and a licence obligation
follows whether or not any version string survived the build.
Measured need: the seven vendor images hold `brctl`, `pppd`, `chat`, `pptp`,
`hdparm`, `hostapd_cli`, `ip`, `tc`, `dhcp6c`, `dhcpcd`, `msntp` and `telnetd`
as standalone binaries while the SBOM named none of them. Four of those
(dhcp6c, dhcpcd, msntp, telnetd) are on the Zyxel vendor notice; several others
are components the commercial reference found and we did not.
Rules for adding entries:
- The key is the installed filename, lowercased. The value is the component,
which is often not the same word: brctl ships in bridge-utils, chat and
pppd in ppp, hostapd_cli in hostapd, ip and tc in iproute2.
- Only add a name you have checked against a real image. A wrong name is
worse than a missing one.
- No versions here either. Nothing about an installed filename gives one.
- No purl or CPE: these judgements carry no version, so they cannot match a
CVE, and an identifier on a versionless component only invites a matcher to
pair it with the wrong advisory.
- Short, common names are the risk. `ip`, `tc` and `chat` are ordinary English
words and a vendor may ship its own. They are kept because the reader only
counts a file that is an ELF executable under bin/ or sbin/, and because the
evidence path is in the artifact for a human to check.
- busybox applets are excluded at read time, not here: an image that installs
`/bin/telnetd` as a copy of busybox is carrying busybox, not telnetd.
Deliberately absent:
ftp   — could be netkit-ftp, tnftp or a vendor client, and the binary in hand
does not say which. Naming one of them would be a guess.
sshd, ssh-keygen — cve-bin-tool already identifies openssh with a version, and
a versionless duplicate adds nothing.
